name: Save the Nature
description: You are an environmental activist at heart but the reality is harsh and you are just a cashier in a cinema. But you can still do something! You have $$$n$$$ tickets to sell. The price of the $$$i$$$-th ticket is $$$p_i$$$. As a teller, you have a possibility to select the order in which the tickets will be sold (i.e. a permutation of the tickets). You know that the cinema participates in two ecological restoration programs applying them to the order you chose : The $$$x\%$$$ of the price of each the $$$a$$$-th sold ticket ($$$a$$$-th, $$$2a$$$-th, $$$3a$$$-th and so on) in the order you chose is aimed for research and spreading of renewable energy sources. The $$$y\%$$$ of the price of each the $$$b$$$-th sold ticket ($$$b$$$-th, $$$2b$$$-th, $$$3b$$$-th and so on) in the order you chose is aimed for pollution abatement. If the ticket is in both programs then the $$$(x + y) \%$$$ are used for environmental activities. Also, it's known that all prices are multiples of $$$100$$$, so there is no need in any rounding. For example, if you'd like to sell tickets with prices $$$[400, 100, 300, 200]$$$ and the cinema pays $$$10\%$$$ of each $$$2$$$-nd sold ticket and $$$20\%$$$ of each $$$3$$$-rd sold ticket, then arranging them in order $$$[100, 200, 300, 400]$$$ will lead to contribution equal to $$$100 \cdot 0 + 200 \cdot 0.1 + 300 \cdot 0.2 + 400 \cdot 0.1 = 120$$$. But arranging them in order $$$[100, 300, 400, 200]$$$ will lead to $$$100 \cdot 0 + 300 \cdot 0.1 + 400 \cdot 0.2 + 200 \cdot 0.1 = 130$$$. Nature can't wait, so you decided to change the order of tickets in such a way, so that the total contribution to programs will reach at least $$$k$$$ in minimum number of sold tickets. Or say that it's impossible to do so. In other words, find the minimum number of tickets which are needed to be sold in order to earn at least $$$k$$$.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \le q \le 100$$$) — the number of independent queries. Each query consists of $$$5$$$ lines. The first line of each query contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of tickets. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$$$ ($$$100 \le p_i \le 10^9$$$, $$$p_i \bmod 100 = 0$$$) — the corresponding prices of tickets. The third line contains two integers $$$x$$$ and $$$a$$$ ($$$1 \le x \le 100$$$, $$$x + y \le 100$$$, $$$1 \le a \le n$$$) — the parameters of the first program. The fourth line contains two integers $$$y$$$ and $$$b$$$ ($$$1 \le y \le 100$$$, $$$x + y \le 100$$$, $$$1 \le b \le n$$$) — the parameters of the second program. The fifth line contains single integer $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \le k \le 10^{14}$$$) — the required total contribution. It's guaranteed that the total number of tickets per test doesn't exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: Print $$$q$$$ integers — one per query. For each query, print the minimum number of tickets you need to sell to make the total ecological contribution of at least $$$k$$$ if you can sell tickets in any order. If the total contribution can not be achieved selling all the tickets, print $$$-1$$$.
approach_summary: Verify predicate monotonicity: P(x) is true for x ≤ K and false otherwise. Binary search over the answer domain to find the boundary in O(log(Range) × Verify_Time).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1223C — Save the Nature [33. Binary Search]
topic_editorial.summary: Binary search on the monotonic answer domain.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The predicate function $P(x)$ ('Is answer $\le x$ feasible?') is monotonic: if $P(x)$ is true for some value, it remains true for all larger values (or vice versa). This allows binary division of the answer search space $[\text{low}, \text{high}]$ in $O(\log(\text{Range}))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N \log(\text{Range}))$
  The binary search divides the search interval by 2 at each iteration, requiring $\log_2(\text{Range})$ steps. In each step, the feasibility check `check(mid)` scans the array in $\mathcal{O}(N)$ time.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(1)$ auxiliary space
  The algorithm operates directly over the input array without allocating extra auxiliary memory.
